The North Carolina health department recommended post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for 213 of the people who were evaluated for potential rabies risk. BSIP SA/Alamy Stock Photo Local health departments in North Carolina have evaluated hundreds of people for rabies after they interacted with baby goats that were part of a mobile petting zoo, according to the state Department of Health and Human Services. As of Wednesday, 284 people have been evaluated by local health departments, while others have consulted with a healthcare provider directly to assess their potential rabies risk. The goats were owned by Farm Adventures, based in Harmony, North Carolina. Between July 28 and August 27, local officials said in a statement, the farm took the goats throughout the state and visited at least 10 locations, including a Masonic picnic, assisted living centers and a back-to-school bash, as well as private events. Ad Feedback Related article Colorized transmission electron micrograph of rabies virus particles (blue). BSIP SA/Alamy Stock Photo Baby goats with rabies at North Carolina mobile petting zoo prompt calls across multiple counties to contact health officials 5 min read The state health department recommended post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for 213 of the people who were evaluated. If started promptly after exposure, PEP is considered 100% effective at preventing a fatal rabies infection. About 100,000 people are treated with PEP each year in the US, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It typically starts with wound care if there was a bite or scratch — rabies can also spread through contact with an animal’s saliva — followed by human rabies immunoglobulin to help fight a potential infection until vaccines take effect. Four or five vaccine doses are given, based on the patient’s weight. In the past, people exposed to rabies received up to 30 painful vaccine shots in the stomach. Today, adults can get the shots in the shoulder muscle, while children can get them in the thigh over the course of 14 days. Side effects are generally mild and may include a sore arm, a headache and an upset stomach. Without prompt treatment, rabies is typically fatal. Symptoms, which can take up to two months to develop, may include headache, nausea and sore throat before progressing to hallucinations, delusions, disorientation, paralysis and coma. Related vertical video Krista Edelman She woke up with a bat on her mouth At Jurney’s Assisted Living Home in Statesville, Executive Director Chrissy Stein-Martin said eight residents are undergoing treatment after interacting with the goats. None refused PEP, she said, and the hospital and health departments have been “great to work with.” “They’ve been asking good questions, seeing what they can do to help. In fact, the health department’s coming here to do all the follow-up vaccines so we don’t have to take the residents out. And the families have been very supportive,” she said. Going forward, Stein-Martin said, the facility will still welcome dog visitors but will no longer host farm animals. Alpacas from a local farm have regularly visited the facility, but when she learned that North Carolina requires rabies vaccines for only cats, dogs and ferrets — not farm animals, including goats – she decided “there’s no reason to put everyone at risk.” Farm Adventures said in a statement that its “4 precious baby goats” that may have exposed people to rabies have been euthanized. Tests detected the virus in three of the goats. The farm said it is monitoring its other animals, but none has become sick. Related vertical video TRIMET These two goats apparently had somewhere to be The baby goats had been kept in a separate pen because they were too young to get vaccinated, according to the farm’s owner, Misty Love, who told CNN on Saturday that a wild skunk had gotten into the baby goats’ pen July 29. The farm shot and burned the skunk. None of the goats appeared to have been bitten, but one died August 19, and another fell ill the next day and had to be euthanized. North Carolina’s health department said it is “well prepared to respond to rabies.” About 300 animals test positive for rabies in the state every year; most of them wild. In 2025, more than 4,000 animals were tested for rabies in North Carolina, and only about 6% were positive for the virus, the health department said. As of August 28, more than 320 people in North Carolina had received PEP, the health department said. That figure covers all rabies exposures in the state, not just people exposed to the infected goats. Since rabies was confirmed in the goats, state and local health authorities and the CDC have coordinated with the farm and local authorities to determine who was exposed and who may need treatment. The state health department said it has been in regular contact with the CDC, and that agency said Monday that it supplied information and tools to support rabies risk assessments. The CDC’s latest rabies exposure surveillance report, released Monday, analyzed cases from 2024 and reported that four people died of rabies that year. Two were exposed to bats and did not receive treatment. Another case involved international travel. There was no information about the fourth case. The state health department said North Carolina has an adequate supply of prophylaxis and would provide it to anyone who needs it. The Mecklenburg County Public Health Department, which had one private event with exposure to the goats, declined to share details about the event or those exposed. Anyone with concerns is urged to contact the department. At Jurney’s, Stein-Martin said, residents have “not been stressed at all” about the experience. Instead, they’ve been making light of it – “maybe even too light,” making goat sounds at each other and joking about not licking people. She said levity is important in a potentially scary situation. In fact, Stein-Martin, who writes psychological thrillers in her spare time, said residents keep encouraging her to write a new book about a rabies scare in an assisted living community. “Unexpectedly, I now feel like I’m 100% qualified to do that,” she said. Learn what to do if you have a bat encounter. Ivan Kuzmin/Adobe Stock By Korin Miller Published on August 31, 2026 Fact-Checked by Emily Kay Votruba Add us on Google ON THIS PAGE Can Touching a Bat Make You Sick? How to Know if a Bat Exposure Is High-Risk or Low-Risk What to Do After a Bat Touches You Should You Go to the ER? How to Prevent Bat-Related Illness ON THIS PAGE ON THIS PAGE Can Touching a Bat Make You Sick? How to Know if a Bat Exposure Is High-Risk or Low-Risk What to Do After a Bat Touches You Should You Go to the ER? How to Prevent Bat-Related Illness The sight of a bat flying through the sky may be harmless, but an up-close encounter is a different story. Just ask Krista Edelman, MD, a gastroenterologist in Virginia, who recently went viral after revealing in an Instagram video that she woke up to find a bat attempting to burrow into her mouth. Dr. Edelman said in her video that she dreamed a mouse was trying to get into her mouth, only to wake up and discover that it was a bat. “I went from thinking I was dreaming to realizing very quickly that this was, in fact, happening,” she said. [1] Edelman’s video comes just a few weeks after an 11-year-old boy in Canada died after waking up to find a bat on his face. Initially, his family didn’t seek medical care for him because there weren’t any visible bites. But he developed symptoms of rabies about 19 days later, and died after two weeks in the hospital. [2] If you come into contact with a bat, it’s essential to get proper medical assessment and treatment. Doctors explain the health risks of touching a bat. Can Touching a Bat Make You Sick? Rabies, a serious viral disease, is the biggest health concern from bat encounters. These flying mammals are the leading source of human rabies cases in the United States. Of the 60,000 Americans who get rabies shots each year, two-thirds do so because of a bat exposure. Among rabies fatalities, at least 7 out of 10 are caused by bats. [3] [4] But the type of bat exposure matters. “Touching a bat’s fur, or contact with bat blood, urine, or droppings, is not by itself considered a rabies exposure and does not require treatment,” says Zoe Weiss, MD, a clinical microbiologist and an infectious disease specialist at Tufts Medical Center in Boston. The situation is different and far more dangerous if the bat’s saliva enters the body through a bite, scratch, or via contact with the eyes, nose, or mouth, she explains. The problem is that it can be difficult to know if a bat has bitten or scratched you, says Neil Modi, MD, an infectious disease physician at Northwell Health Primary and Specialty Care at Chappaqua Crossing, New York. “Because bat bites and scratches can be easily missed and wounds can often be minuscule, many people do not realize they have been scratched or bitten,” he explains. As a result, “any direct physical contact with a bat should be evaluated by a health professional rather than dismissed,” Dr. Weiss says. Rabies is almost always fatal in humans if it’s not treated promptly after an exposure. But the virus that causes rabies cannot be transmitted from person to person. How to Know if a Bat Exposure Is High-Risk or Low-Risk Healthcare providers typically categorize bat exposures as high-risk or low-risk. High-Risk Bat Exposures Common high-risk exposures are waking up to find a bat flying around your bedroom or a bat flying into you, according to John Crane, MD, PhD, a professor of medicine in the division of infectious diseases at the State University of New York at Buffalo. In this situation, you can’t rule out the possibility that the bat has touched, scratched, or bitten you, he explains. It’s also concerning if a bat flies into you, because it suggests something is wrong with the animal. “Bats have excellent echolocation and navigation skills — they are very adept flyers and are not clumsy when healthy,” says Christopher Bazzoli, MD, an emergency medicine physician at Cleveland Clinic. “A normal bat will not collide with a human, even if inside a home.” Finding a bat near an unattended child is also considered a high-risk exposure if the bat cannot be tested, Dr. Modi says. “As far as your pets, finding a bat near your pet does not necessarily qualify as a human exposure,” he says. "It does qualify as a pet exposure. Your pet should be taken to your veterinarian for a thorough assessment.” Low-Risk Bat Exposures If you see a bat outdoors, it’s considered a low-risk encounter and does not require treatment, Dr. Crane says. “If you had a bat in your garage, opened the door, and the bat flew out, that would be low-risk,” he says. Touching a bat’s fur is considered low-risk as well, as long as you can rule out a bite or scratch, Modi says. But you should never pick up a bat with your bare hands, he notes. What to Do Immediately After a Bat Touches You It is typically considered a high-risk exposure if a bat touches you (even if you can’t see a wound), bites you, or tries to get in your mouth. “Wash the site immediately and thoroughly with soap and water for several minutes,” Weiss says. “Immediate wound washing alone substantially reduces rabies risk.” Consider Trying to Catch the Bat to Be Tested for Rabies If you’re indoors and able to safely capture the bat that touched you, doctors recommend trying to catch it so health officials can test it for rabies. “If the bat can be safely captured and tested, and the result is negative, post-exposure treatment can be avoided entirely, or stopped if already started,” Weiss says. She suggests the following for safety while trying to capture a bat: Wear thick gloves. Do not try to touch the bat with bare hands. Use a box or coffee can. When the bat lands, cover it with a container, slide cardboard underneath to trap the animal and tape the container closed with air holes. Contact local animal control or your local health department. They can arrange testing and determine if treatment is needed. Preserve the bat for testing. “Do not release it and try not to damage the head, which is needed for the test,” Weiss says. “Never attempt to keep or relocate a live bat.” Should You Go to the ER if a Bat Touches You? It is important to seek medical care quickly after a physical encounter with a bat. Weiss suggests contacting your local health department and going to the emergency room for a rabies shot and immunoglobulin, an emergency medicine made from human blood that delivers short-term antibodies to help neutralize the rabies virus. Weiss says it’s better to go to an ER than an urgent care facility, since ERs are more likely to have the treatment you’ll need. “Not all locations will carry the rabies immunoglobulin, so it does also help to either call ahead to the location to check if they have it, or call your local health department. They can usually direct people to a nearby site known to stock rabies treatment, which is often faster than calling around,” she says. During a medical evaluation, your healthcare provider will assess your risk by getting a detailed history of the exposure to determine if treatment is needed, per Modi. “They will also assess the wound and provide local wound care,” he says. “Often, a public health official will be contacted as well to assist with the assessment.” Post-exposure prophylaxis (or PEP), the shots you get to prevent rabies infection, “should begin as soon as possible after exposure, ideally the same day, although it should still be given even after a delay,” Weiss says. “Rabies is essentially fatal once the disease reaches the central nervous system,” says Dr. Bazzoli. “That being said, the process of tissue exposure to infection, and that infection spreading to the central nervous system, takes days — our best data indicate a week or more. This is why we think of rabies exposure as a medical urgency, and typically not an emergency.” Are Rabies Shots Painful? You may have heard that rabies vaccination involves a painful shot in the stomach, but those are a thing of the past. “That hasn’t been the case for more than 20 years, and it’s a dangerous myth,” Crane says. “This is a regular injection in your arm, like a flu shot.” The rabies vaccine is often a series of shots in the arm, according to Modi. “Depending on if you have been vaccinated in the past, the number of shots can range from two to four,” he says. “Additionally, your healthcare provider may determine you need locally administered rabies immunoglobulin, depending on your medical history, vaccination history, and the details of your exposure.” How to Prevent Bat-Related Illness There are a few things you can do to lower your chances of a high-risk bat encounter. Try to keep bats out of your living spaces. That means sealing any potential entry points for wildlife, such as vents, chimneys, or windows, Modi says. Don’t handle bats. “Never directly touch or handle a bat,” Modi says. Vaccinate pets against rabies. This "maintains a barrier between wildlife and people,” Weiss says. Learn what to do if you have a bat encounter. Ivan Kuzmin/Adobe Stock By Korin Miller Published on August 31, 2026 Fact-Checked by Emily Kay Votruba Add us on Google ON THIS PAGE Can Touching a Bat Make You Sick? How to Know if a Bat Exposure Is High-Risk or Low-Risk What to Do After a Bat Touches You Should You Go to the ER? How to Prevent Bat-Related Illness ON THIS PAGE ON THIS PAGE Can Touching a Bat Make You Sick? How to Know if a Bat Exposure Is High-Risk or Low-Risk What to Do After a Bat Touches You Should You Go to the ER? How to Prevent Bat-Related Illness The sight of a bat flying through the sky may be harmless, but an up-close encounter is a different story. Just ask Krista Edelman, MD, a gastroenterologist in Virginia, who recently went viral after revealing in an Instagram video that she woke up to find a bat attempting to burrow into her mouth. Dr. Edelman said in her video that she dreamed a mouse was trying to get into her mouth, only to wake up and discover that it was a bat. “I went from thinking I was dreaming to realizing very quickly that this was, in fact, happening,” she said. [1] Edelman’s video comes just a few weeks after an 11-year-old boy in Canada died after waking up to find a bat on his face. Initially, his family didn’t seek medical care for him because there weren’t any visible bites. But he developed symptoms of rabies about 19 days later, and died after two weeks in the hospital. [2] If you come into contact with a bat, it’s essential to get proper medical assessment and treatment. Doctors explain the health risks of touching a bat. Can Touching a Bat Make You Sick? Rabies, a serious viral disease, is the biggest health concern from bat encounters. These flying mammals are the leading source of human rabies cases in the United States. Of the 60,000 Americans who get rabies shots each year, two-thirds do so because of a bat exposure. Among rabies fatalities, at least 7 out of 10 are caused by bats. [3] [4] But the type of bat exposure matters. “Touching a bat’s fur, or contact with bat blood, urine, or droppings, is not by itself considered a rabies exposure and does not require treatment,” says Zoe Weiss, MD, a clinical microbiologist and an infectious disease specialist at Tufts Medical Center in Boston. The situation is different and far more dangerous if the bat’s saliva enters the body through a bite, scratch, or via contact with the eyes, nose, or mouth, she explains. The problem is that it can be difficult to know if a bat has bitten or scratched you, says Neil Modi, MD, an infectious disease physician at Northwell Health Primary and Specialty Care at Chappaqua Crossing, New York. “Because bat bites and scratches can be easily missed and wounds can often be minuscule, many people do not realize they have been scratched or bitten,” he explains. As a result, “any direct physical contact with a bat should be evaluated by a health professional rather than dismissed,” Dr. Weiss says. Rabies is almost always fatal in humans if it’s not treated promptly after an exposure. But the virus that causes rabies cannot be transmitted from person to person. How to Know if a Bat Exposure Is High-Risk or Low-Risk Healthcare providers typically categorize bat exposures as high-risk or low-risk. High-Risk Bat Exposures Common high-risk exposures are waking up to find a bat flying around your bedroom or a bat flying into you, according to John Crane, MD, PhD, a professor of medicine in the division of infectious diseases at the State University of New York at Buffalo. In this situation, you can’t rule out the possibility that the bat has touched, scratched, or bitten you, he explains. It’s also concerning if a bat flies into you, because it suggests something is wrong with the animal. “Bats have excellent echolocation and navigation skills — they are very adept flyers and are not clumsy when healthy,” says Christopher Bazzoli, MD, an emergency medicine physician at Cleveland Clinic. “A normal bat will not collide with a human, even if inside a home.” Finding a bat near an unattended child is also considered a high-risk exposure if the bat cannot be tested, Dr. Modi says. “As far as your pets, finding a bat near your pet does not necessarily qualify as a human exposure,” he says. "It does qualify as a pet exposure. Your pet should be taken to your veterinarian for a thorough assessment.” Low-Risk Bat Exposures If you see a bat outdoors, it’s considered a low-risk encounter and does not require treatment, Dr. Crane says. “If you had a bat in your garage, opened the door, and the bat flew out, that would be low-risk,” he says. Touching a bat’s fur is considered low-risk as well, as long as you can rule out a bite or scratch, Modi says. But you should never pick up a bat with your bare hands, he notes. What to Do Immediately After a Bat Touches You It is typically considered a high-risk exposure if a bat touches you (even if you can’t see a wound), bites you, or tries to get in your mouth. “Wash the site immediately and thoroughly with soap and water for several minutes,” Weiss says. “Immediate wound washing alone substantially reduces rabies risk.” Consider Trying to Catch the Bat to Be Tested for Rabies If you’re indoors and able to safely capture the bat that touched you, doctors recommend trying to catch it so health officials can test it for rabies. “If the bat can be safely captured and tested, and the result is negative, post-exposure treatment can be avoided entirely, or stopped if already started,” Weiss says. She suggests the following for safety while trying to capture a bat: Wear thick gloves. Do not try to touch the bat with bare hands. Use a box or coffee can. When the bat lands, cover it with a container, slide cardboard underneath to trap the animal and tape the container closed with air holes. Contact local animal control or your local health department. They can arrange testing and determine if treatment is needed. Preserve the bat for testing. “Do not release it and try not to damage the head, which is needed for the test,” Weiss says. “Never attempt to keep or relocate a live bat.” Should You Go to the ER if a Bat Touches You? It is important to seek medical care quickly after a physical encounter with a bat. Weiss suggests contacting your local health department and going to the emergency room for a rabies shot and immunoglobulin, an emergency medicine made from human blood that delivers short-term antibodies to help neutralize the rabies virus. Weiss says it’s better to go to an ER than an urgent care facility, since ERs are more likely to have the treatment you’ll need. “Not all locations will carry the rabies immunoglobulin, so it does also help to either call ahead to the location to check if they have it, or call your local health department. They can usually direct people to a nearby site known to stock rabies treatment, which is often faster than calling around,” she says. During a medical evaluation, your healthcare provider will assess your risk by getting a detailed history of the exposure to determine if treatment is needed, per Modi. “They will also assess the wound and provide local wound care,” he says. “Often, a public health official will be contacted as well to assist with the assessment.” Post-exposure prophylaxis (or PEP), the shots you get to prevent rabies infection, “should begin as soon as possible after exposure, ideally the same day, although it should still be given even after a delay,” Weiss says. “Rabies is essentially fatal once the disease reaches the central nervous system,” says Dr. Bazzoli. “That being said, the process of tissue exposure to infection, and that infection spreading to the central nervous system, takes days — our best data indicate a week or more. This is why we think of rabies exposure as a medical urgency, and typically not an emergency.” Are Rabies Shots Painful? You may have heard that rabies vaccination involves a painful shot in the stomach, but those are a thing of the past. “That hasn’t been the case for more than 20 years, and it’s a dangerous myth,” Crane says. “This is a regular injection in your arm, like a flu shot.” The rabies vaccine is often a series of shots in the arm, according to Modi. “Depending on if you have been vaccinated in the past, the number of shots can range from two to four,” he says. “Additionally, your healthcare provider may determine you need locally administered rabies immunoglobulin, depending on your medical history, vaccination history, and the details of your exposure.” How to Prevent Bat-Related Illness There are a few things you can do to lower your chances of a high-risk bat encounter. Try to keep bats out of your living spaces. That means sealing any potential entry points for wildlife, such as vents, chimneys, or windows, Modi says. Don’t handle bats. “Never directly touch or handle a bat,” Modi says. Vaccinate pets against rabies. This "maintains a barrier between wildlife and people,” Weiss says. news.content: News Space Sports Restaurants Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals LOCAL Brevard County health officials warn of rabies, West Nile risks Jim Waymer Florida Today Sept. 3, 2026, 12:06 p.m. ET Health officials in Brevard County, Florida, have issued warnings for both West Nile virus and rabies. A rabies alert was issued after a raccoon captured in Melbourne tested positive for the virus. Officials advise residents to avoid wild animals, secure pets, and take precautions against mosquito bites. Florida health officials warned Thursday about risks to Brevard County residents from rabies and the West Nile virus. Several sentinel chickens within the county have recently tested positive for West Nile virus, triggering a health advisory. Thursday's rabies alert was in response to a confirmed case of rabies in a raccoon that was captured in the Melbourne area off Andrews Avenue on Aug. 27. State health officials and Brevard County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts "by enhanced monitoring for mosquitoes and diseases as well as targeted mosquito treatment and overnight spraying to reduce the risk of disease transmission," FDOH said in a release. State and county officials continue to conduct statewide surveillance for mosquito-borne illnesses,including West Nile virus infections, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria,chikungunya and dengue. Health officials urge the public to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes by taking basic precautions, such as avoiding being outdoors at dawn and dusk, using mosquito repellants and/or wearing long-sleaves and pants to cover the skin. Residents also are encouraged to report dead birds to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s website: myfwc.com/research/wildlife/health/avian. Brevard health officials issue Sept. 3 rabies alert On Thursday (Sept. 3) state health officials issued a rabies alert in Brevard in response to a confirmed case of the viral infection in a raccoon that was captured in the Melbourne area off Andrews Avenue on Aug. 27. "People and domestic animals should always avoid physical contact with wild animals," Florida health officials warned in a press release. That includes raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes, which carry a higher risk of human exposure and a need for rabies post-exposure treatment. "If you are exposed to rabies, receiving appropriate treatment after exposure will protect you from the risk of rabies." The rabies alert is for 60 days and includes the following boundaries in Brevard County: Northern boundary: West Eau Gallie Boulevard Southern boundary: Sarno Road Eastern boundary: Croton Road Western boundary: North Wickham Road Immunize your pets and livestock based on your veterinarian’s recommended schedule. news.content_original: News Space Sports Restaurants Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals LOCAL Brevard County health officials warn of rabies, West Nile risks Jim Waymer Florida Today Sept. 3, 2026, 12:06 p.m. ET Health officials in Brevard County, Florida, have issued warnings for both West Nile virus and rabies. A rabies alert was issued after a raccoon captured in Melbourne tested positive for the virus. Officials advise residents to avoid wild animals, secure pets, and take precautions against mosquito bites. Florida health officials warned Thursday about risks to Brevard County residents from rabies and the West Nile virus. Several sentinel chickens within the county have recently tested positive for West Nile virus, triggering a health advisory. Thursday's rabies alert was in response to a confirmed case of rabies in a raccoon that was captured in the Melbourne area off Andrews Avenue on Aug. 27. State health officials and Brevard County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts "by enhanced monitoring for mosquitoes and diseases as well as targeted mosquito treatment and overnight spraying to reduce the risk of disease transmission," FDOH said in a release. State and county officials continue to conduct statewide surveillance for mosquito-borne illnesses,including West Nile virus infections, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria,chikungunya and dengue. Health officials urge the public to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes by taking basic precautions, such as avoiding being outdoors at dawn and dusk, using mosquito repellants and/or wearing long-sleaves and pants to cover the skin. Residents also are encouraged to report dead birds to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s website: myfwc.com/research/wildlife/health/avian. Brevard health officials issue Sept. 3 rabies alert On Thursday (Sept. 3) state health officials issued a rabies alert in Brevard in response to a confirmed case of the viral infection in a raccoon that was captured in the Melbourne area off Andrews Avenue on Aug. 27. "People and domestic animals should always avoid physical contact with wild animals," Florida health officials warned in a press release. That includes raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes, which carry a higher risk of human exposure and a need for rabies post-exposure treatment. "If you are exposed to rabies, receiving appropriate treatment after exposure will protect you from the risk of rabies." The rabies alert is for 60 days and includes the following boundaries in Brevard County: Northern boundary: West Eau Gallie Boulevard Southern boundary: Sarno Road Eastern boundary: Croton Road Western boundary: North Wickham Road Immunize your pets and livestock based on your veterinarian’s recommended schedule. Avoid contact with wild or stray animals. Do not handle, feed, or unintentionally attract them with outdoor pet food, open garbage cans, or other sources of food. If you have been bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal, seek medical attention, and report the injury to DOH-Brevard by calling 321-634-6337 option 3. Never adopt wild animals or bring them into your home; instead, contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. Prevent wildlife, including bats, from entering living quarters or occupied spaces in homes, schools, and other similar areas where they might come in contact with people and pets. Subscribe More forecasts: Atlanta 30 day forecast Atlanta/ Crime & Emergencies Rabid Bat Found Dead Inside Snellville Home, Officials Can't Confirm Any Human Contact By Ray Bianchi Published on September 05, 2026 Source: Google Street View A bat found dead inside a home near Stockton Walk Lane in Snellville has tested positive for rabies, prompting Gwinnett County officials to issue a public advisory urging residents to steer clear of stray or unusually behaving animals. The bat was discovered on August 28, and officials say they have not been able to confirm whether any humans or household pets came into direct contact with it before it died. The discovery, first reported by FOX 5 Atlanta, has left investigators without answers on a key question: how the bat got into the home in the first place. That detail remains undetermined, according to the outlet, which cited a press release from Gwinnett County government. Gwinnett County Animal Welfare and Enforcement issued the advisory alongside the confirmed test result, warning pet owners to keep their animals current on rabies vaccinations. Why Bats Are the Biggest Rabies Threat Bats and foxes are among the wild animals capable of carrying and transmitting the virus, and nationally, bats are responsible for roughly 70% of fatal human rabies cases acquired in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Rabies spreads to humans and pets through bites or scratches from infected wildlife, and once symptoms appear, the virus is almost always fatal in humans if preventive treatment isn't given immediately, per the CDC. The virus attacks the central nervous system, and early symptoms in people can include fever, headache, and general weakness or discomfort. That danger is part of why Gwinnett County Animal Welfare and Enforcement Director Katrina Hellman has previously urged residents to call animal control rather than pest control if a bat turns up inside a home, warning that a sleeping person could be bitten without ever feeling it or noticing a mark, according to WSB Radio. The county recorded 10 confirmed animal rabies cases in 2024, with a slight decrease in confirmed cases in 2025, per the same report. What to Do After a Possible Exposure Officials say anyone bitten or scratched by a stray or suspected rabid animal should seek medical care immediately and tell their healthcare provider about the exposure. The standard post-exposure regimen for unvaccinated people recommended by the CDC includes thorough wound washing, one dose of human rabies immune globulin, and four doses of rabies vaccine given on days 0, 3, 7, and 14. Pets face their own protocol. Unvaccinated dogs or cats exposed to a rabid animal must undergo a strict four-month quarantine and receive a rabies vaccination one month before release, according to NASPHV guidelines cited in the FOX 5 Atlanta report. Separately, Gwinnett County ordinances require any dog, cat, or ferret that bites or scratches a person to undergo a mandatory 10-day quarantine observation, per Gwinnett County. Georgia law also mandates that all dogs, cats, and ferrets 12 weeks or older be vaccinated against rabies by a licensed veterinarian, under Georgia Code § 31-19-5. Anyone who believes they were exposed to a suspected rabid animal can contact GNR Public Health at 770-339-4260. Residents who spot an animal behaving unusually, or who need one picked up, can call the Gwinnett Animal Welfare and Enforcement bite office at 770-339-3200, ext. 5576. Part of a Wider Pattern Across Gwinnett The Snellville case is the latest in a string of wildlife rabies alerts across the county this year. In July, officials reported a raccoon near Biltmore Oaks Drive in Bethlehem had tested positive after attacking a dog in May, according to 11Alive. Hoodline has also tracked a rabid coyote in Buford and reported on a rabid raccoon that mauled a dog in Dacula. A retrospective study of Georgia rabies laboratory data from 2010 to 2021 found wildlife made up 93.7% of confirmed positive cases statewide, with raccoons accounting for 68.9% and bats making up 2.7% of positive specimens, according to a report published on PubMed Central. Domestic animals accounted for only 6.3% of positive submissions over that period, underscoring how mandatory pet vaccination laws have shifted the state's rabies risk almost entirely onto wildlife. news.content: Kitten in Jacksonville, raccoon in Taneytown test positive for rabies, health officials warn Rabies virus, illustration. Rabies virus is a member of the Rhabdoviridae family. This bullet-shaped enveloped virus has a protein coat (capsid), which is made up of helically arranged subunits called capsomeres and covered with surface glycoprotein spikes. Within the coat is the genetic material in the form of single-stranded ribonucleic acid (RNA). The rabies virus is transmitted to humans from an infected animal bite. Symptoms appear after an incubation period of 10 days to 1 year and include fever, breathing difficulties, muscle spasms, and hydrophobia SOURCE: Kateryna Kon/Science Photo Library via Getty Images Advertisement Updated: 2:26 PM EDT Sep 2, 2026 Editorial Standards i Greg Ng Digital Content Manager Kitten in Jacksonville, raccoon in Taneytown test positive for rabies, health officials warn Updated: 2:26 PM EDT Sep 2, 2026 Editorial Standards i Greg Ng Digital Content Manager TANEYTOWN, Md. — A raccoon in the Taneytown area and a kitten in Jacksonville tested positive for rabies , health officials announced Wednesday. Carroll County health officials said Animal Control was called to York Street near Maryland Route 140 on Aug. 27 for an aggressive raccoon that was killed by a dog. Advertisement Health officials said they're concerned that other pets or people in the area may have been exposed to the infected raccoon before its death. "Rabies exposure occurs through bites and scratches or saliva from the infected animal getting into the eyes, nose, mouth, or a wound of a person or another animal," Joe Mancuso, the Carroll County Health Department's rabies program manager, said in a statement. Anyone who may have been exposed or whose pet may have been exposed to bites, scratches, or saliva from this raccoon can call the health department at 410-876-1884 for a risk assessment. In Baltimore County, health officials announced that a kitten found in the 3300 block of Paper Mill Road tested positive Tuesday for rabies. The animal was an approximately 16‐week‐old orange domestic medium-haired male. Baltimore County Animal Services said there was one human exposure and officials are notifying caretakers of registered community cat colonies in the area. The Baltimore County Department of Health should be contacted if direct exposure occurred involving bites, scratches, or licks. Call 410‐887‐5963 during business hours, or 410‐832‐7182 after hours. Immediate medical evaluation is recommended for anyone who may have had contact with the affected animals. "Rabies is a preventable disease, but only when exposures are reported promptly and vaccination practices are followed," BCAS Bureau Director Dr. René Varela said in a statement. "Incidents like this highlight the importance of avoiding contact with unfamiliar animals and ensuring that pets remain current on their rabies vaccinations. Maintaining vigilance in the community is essential to protecting both animal and human health." Health officials offered the following information to help keep yourself, your family and your pets safe from rabies. Do not approach, handle, pet or feed wild or stray animals. Have your dogs, cats and ferrets vaccinated against rabies and keep their vaccinations up to date. Do not leave pets outside unattended or allow them to roam free. Cover garbage cans tightly and do not leave pet food outside. Teach children to stay away from wild animals and any animals that they do not know. Prevent bats from entering your home by using window screens and chimney caps. Bats found in the home should be safely collected, if possible, and tested for rabies. The Carroll County Health Department's next low-cost rabies vaccination clinic is scheduled for 2-4 p.m. on Sept. 20 at the Ag Center in Westminster. news.content: Rabid bat found in Cascade County Posted on September 1, 2026 by Jenn Rowell A bat in Cascade County tested positive for rabies, and health officials are reminding locals to be aware of the risk for rabies exposure. On Aug. 28, the Cascade City-County Health Department confirmed the positive rabies test. Trisha Gardner, county health officer, told The Electric that the bat was found near a local pet cat and there was concern that the cat had killed the bat, or otherwise been scratched or bitten by the bat. Pets can become infected by biting bats, she said. Bird flu detected in Gibson Park goose; waterfowl roundup postponed [2025] The cat owner took the vaccinated cat to the vet for a rabies booster shot and also brought the bat, which the vet sent off for testing, Gardner said. Pets can only be tested for rabies post-mortem, which means after the animal has died. Gardner said that in incidents involving pets and bats, they check the pet’s vaccination status to determine next steps. If the animal is vaccinated, no further action is typically needed. CCHD confirms rabid bat in Cascade County [2024] If an animal is not vaccinated, health officials may quarantine or euthanize it, depending on the circumstances. Gardner said it’s difficult to see bat bites on humans, and even more difficult to see bat bites or scratches on animals. Rabies is a fatal disease. The rabies virus is carried in the saliva of infected warm-blooded mammals and is usually transmitted to people and other animals through a bite. FWP detects fungus in bats in Cascade County cave [2023] Human rabies deaths in the U.S. are rare, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control, and average one to two deaths per year since the 1990s. Preventive treatment for rabies is nearly 100 percent successful; the last identified human death in Montana occurred in 1997. Rabid bat confirmed in Cascade County [2021] Rabies is preventable and CCHD recommends following these tips: do not feed or handle wild animals, especially bats. Bats and skunks are the most likely carriers of the rabies virus in Montana and should be completely avoided. Bats are especially concerning because their teeth are so small that a bite may not be noticeable. avoid animal bites from domestic animals. Never approach an animal at large and always ask the owner’s permission before petting an animal. Another common source of bite exposures is attempting to help a sick or injured wild animal. vaccinate dogs and cats against rabies. Cats are especially susceptible to rabies, and all dogs and cats should have a current rabies certificate. If pets have not been vaccinated and are potentially exposed to rabies, they could be put down. bat-proof your house. Bats must not be allowed in living areas of your home. Put screens on all windows, doors, and chimneys to prevent bat entry. know what to do if you catch a suspected animal: if you do catch a bat, or other animal suspected of having rabies, do your best not to damage the head. The brain is needed for the rabies test. know what to do if there’s a bite. If someone is bitten by a domestic dog, cat, or ferret, the animal can be observed for signs of rabies, almost always avoiding the need for treatment. If you are bitten by an animal that cannot be located, observed, or tested, a person may need to undergo a series of shots to prevent rabies. If you are bitten, call a health provider or CCHD immediately. Cascade County Great Falls Health Public Safety

An urgent rabies alert is active across several North Carolina counties after three baby goats at a mobile petting zoo tested positive for the virus. By Jada Harris Published: Aug. 31, 2026 at 2:23 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google RALEIGH, N.C. (WECT) - An urgent rabies alert is active across several North Carolina counties after three baby goats at a mobile petting zoo tested positive for the virus. The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Agriculture & Consumer Services announced three baby goats from Farm Adventures in Harmony tested positive for the virus, with a fourth also presumed to be infected. Health officials said the goats were likely exposed to the virus by a skunk that entered their pen in late July. Officials added no other animals on the farm are believed to pose a risk. NCDHHS officials explained they learned of the potential exposure on Aug. 27, and the NC State Laboratory of Public Health confirmed the presence of the rabies virus in three of the baby goats on Aug. 28. NCDHHS officials ask anyone who had contact with the goats at the Harmony location or at off-site events between July 28 and Aug. 27 to contact their local health department to determine if preventative treatment is necessary. Rabies is fatal if left untreated, but preventable if medication is administered before symptoms begin. Public exposure sites span several counties and include Jurney’s Assisted Living in Statesville (July 28), the Back-to-School Bash in Lexington (Aug. 1), Brookdale Peachtree in Statesville (Aug. 6), and the Masonic Picnic Grounds in Mocksville (Aug. 15), alongside several private events in Mecklenburg, Watauga, Burke, Durham, and Iredell counties. Public health officials confirm they are working with event organizers to notify attendees who may have come into contact with the infected goats at these events. The investigation is ongoing and additional information about potential exposure locations at public events will be released when available. Human rabies infections are extremely rare in the U.S., with North Carolina’s last reported human case occurring in 2011. For more information, click here. Copyright 2026 WECT. All rights reserved. A Bay Area native, Tim has been a part of the CBS Bay Area newsroom for more than two decades and joined the digital staff in 2006. Read Full Bio Tim Fang September 3, 2026 / 8:29 AM PDT / CBS Sacramento Add CBS News on Google Officials at Yosemite National Park said that a bat found dead in Yosemite Valley earlier this year had rabies. In a statement Wednesday, park officials confirmed that a "dead big brown bat" tested positive. The bat was found outside the Curry Village Showerhouse on May 18. Officials said no human contact with the infected bat has been reported. Visitors who may have had direct contact with a bat in Curry Village around that time are urged to contact the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) and their healthcare provider. "Bat bites and scratches can be very small and may not always be visible or painful. Direct contact with a bat also includes on top of clothing or if a wing brushes the skin or hair," park officials said. The bat was the second one in a year to have tested positive for rabies in Yosemite, with the last rabies-positive bat being discovered in July 2025. Officials said a "very small percentage" of bats tested from the park each year have rabies. Yosemite is home to 17 species of bats, according to the park. Park officials urged visitors not to touch or handle bats or other wild animals. Anyone who encounters a bat, dead or alive, should keep their distance and notify park staff. A rare but serious disease, rabies is caused by the rabies virus, which infects the brain. People and animals almost always die once symptoms begin, but the disease is preventable if one seeks medical care right away. According to CDPH, rabies has been reported in 17 people in California since 1980, with the most recent case in 2024. OffOn Stream on After hiring company with infected goats, mom speaks out on possible rabies exposure The goats tested positive for rabies after traveling to events in the state. ByABC11 Raleigh September 2, 2026, 3:23 PM Share A North Carolina mother is speaking out after she hired a mobile petting zoo at the center of a rabies alert affecting baby goats. The goats tested positive for the deadly disease after traveling to events in Durham and other counties across the state. Aylin Cruz says she hired Farm Adventures for her 9-year-old and 4-year-old's birthdays. A few days after the party, Cruz says she received a call from the health department alerting her to possible rabies exposure. State officials say four goats from Farm Adventures Mobile Petting Zoo were likely exposed by a skunk that went into the pen where they're kept. The goats may have come into direct contact with people between July 28 and Aug. 27, raising concern about possible exposure. The owner of the company says all her animals have gotten a rabies booster and so have the people who work at the farm. "I told her, for my peace of mind, and your peace of mind, go get vaccinated, and for any parent that has any question, I highly recommend them to go get vaccinated," she said. State officials say there've been no human rabies cases in North Carolina since 2011. They say if you think you've been exposed, contact your local county health department. OffOn Stream on After hiring company with infected goats, mom speaks out on possible rabies exposure The goats tested positive for rabies after traveling to events in the state. ByABC11 Raleigh September 2, 2026, 3:23 PM Share A North Carolina mother is speaking out after she hired a mobile petting zoo at the center of a rabies alert affecting baby goats. The goats tested positive for the deadly disease after traveling to events in Durham and other counties across the state. Aylin Cruz says she hired Farm Adventures for her 9-year-old and 4-year-old's birthdays. A few days after the party, Cruz says she received a call from the health department alerting her to possible rabies exposure. State officials say four goats from Farm Adventures Mobile Petting Zoo were likely exposed by a skunk that went into the pen where they're kept. The goats may have come into direct contact with people between July 28 and Aug. 27, raising concern about possible exposure. The owner of the company says all her animals have gotten a rabies booster and so have the people who work at the farm. news.content_title: North Carolina Petting Zoo Visitors Warned After 3 Baby Goats Test Positive for Rabies
news.content: Anyone who recently held, fed or cuddled baby goats from a mobile petting zoo in North Carolina may have been exposed to rabies. Three of the goats tested positive, while a fourth was not tested but is assumed to have been infected. The goats came from Farm Adventures in Harmony, North Carolina. They were also taken to several public and private events across the state between July 28 and Aug. 27. The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services believes a skunk entered the goats' pen in late July and exposed them to the virus. Farm Adventures said the goats were too young to receive rabies vaccinations and showed no symptoms. The four goats, named Molly, Maggie, Cow and Uno, were euthanized (as reported on a Facebook post that is on longer available). Based on the information gathered on Aug. 28, health officials determined that no other animals at the farm pose a rabies exposure risk to people. NCDHHS has identified 10 potential exposure events in seven counties. The list includes assisted living facilities in Statesville, a back-to-school event in Lexington and a community event at the Masonic Picnic Grounds in Mocksville. The goats also attended private events in Mecklenburg, Watauga, Burke, Durham and Iredell counties. Public health workers are contacting organizers and attendees who may have interacted with the animals. Anyone who visited Farm Adventures or came into contact with its baby goats at an event between July 28 and Aug. 27 should contact their local health department. Rabies can spread through a bite or scratch. It can also spread if saliva from an infected animal gets into someone's eyes, nose or mouth or touches broken skin. The risk of catching rabies from livestock is lower than the risk from a wild animal bite. However, baby goats are often bottle-fed, carried and cuddled, which could bring people into contact with their saliva. Human rabies is extremely rare in the United States, and North Carolina has not reported a human case since 2011. NCDHHS is asking anyone who may have been exposed to call their local health department before visiting an emergency room or urgent care clinic. This way, staff can evaluate the person's risk and explain whether preventive medication is needed before exposing others. Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms begin, but it can be prevented when treatment starts before that happens. Symptoms can take weeks or months to appear, so people should not wait until they feel sick before calling. Want more articles like this one? analysis.brief_en: In North Carolina, three baby goats from a mobile petting zoo tested positive for rabies, with a fourth assumed to be infected. The goats were exposed to the virus when a skunk entered their pen in late July. The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services (NCDHHS) identified 10 potential exposure events across seven counties, including public and private gatherings. While the risk of rabies from livestock is lower than from wild animals, contact with saliva from infected animals can still pose a threat. NCDHHS is urging anyone who may have been exposed to contact their local health department for evaluation and possible preventive treatment. Public health workers are reaching out to event organizers and attendees to assess potential risks and ensure proper follow-up. The agency emphasized that symptoms may take weeks or months to appear, so prompt action is critical to prevent further spread.

news.content: A mobile petting zoo in North Carolina is at the center of a growing health scare after four of its baby goats tested positive for rabies, and officials are urging anyone who touched them to seek medical guidance immediately. The goats belonged to Farm Adventures, a traveling petting zoo based in Harmony, North Carolina. According to the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, the goats were most likely exposed to rabies by a skunk that entered their pen in late July. Lab testing found the virus in three of the four baby goats, and the fourth was also assumed to have been infected. All four were sadly euthanized to prevent the virus from spreading further. 🐶 SIGN UP to get "pawsitivity" delivered right to your inbox with inspiring & entertaining stories about our furry & feathered friends 🐾🐾 The goats reportedly had sweet, ordinary names—Molly, Maggie, Cow, and Uno—which make the situation feel even more heartbreaking for anyone who may have bottle-fed or cuddled them during a visit. The concern extends well beyond the zoo's home base, as the goats traveled to multiple North Carolina communities, including two stops in Durham County, as well as Statesville, Lexington, Watauga County, Burke County and Mocksville, all between July 28 and Aug. 27. Exposure may have happened at 10 different locations, including an assisted living facility and a back-to-school event. Related: Baby Pygmy Hippo Born at Edinburgh Zoo Is the Roundest Little Meatball Rabies is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear, which is why health officials are treating this seriously. Because baby goats are frequently bottle-fed, handled closely or cuddled, public health officials are working proactively to ensure anyone who has had direct contact with the affected animals is evaluated, since even saliva contact carries some risk of exposure. The good news is that North Carolina has not reported a human rabies case since 2011, and treatment given before symptoms develop is highly effective at preventing infection. Anyone who visited Farm Adventures or one of its off-site events during the exposure window is encouraged to contact their local health department to determine whether preventive treatment is needed. Farm Adventures has also set up a call center at 336-242-2371 to help answer questions from concerned visitors. For pet and animal lovers, this story is a good reminder that even the cuddliest, most harmless-looking animals can carry serious risks, and that a quick call to a health official is always worth it if there's any doubt. supplementary_news.content: Rumors Stats Odds Betting Newsletter LOCAL Brevard County health officials warn of rabies, West Nile risks Jim Waymer Florida Today Sept. 3, 2026, 12:06 p.m. ET Health officials in Brevard County, Florida, have issued warnings for both West Nile virus and rabies. A rabies alert was issued after a raccoon captured in Melbourne tested positive for the virus. Officials advise residents to avoid wild animals, secure pets, and take precautions against mosquito bites. Florida health officials warned Thursday about risks to Brevard County residents from rabies and the West Nile virus. Several sentinel chickens within the county have recently tested positive for West Nile virus, triggering a health advisory. Thursday's rabies alert was in response to a confirmed case of rabies in a raccoon that was captured in the Melbourne area off Andrews Avenue on Aug. 27. State health officials and Brevard County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts "by enhanced monitoring for mosquitoes and diseases as well as targeted mosquito treatment and overnight spraying to reduce the risk of disease transmission," FDOH said in a release. State and county officials continue to conduct statewide surveillance for mosquito-borne illnesses,including West Nile virus infections, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria,chikungunya and dengue. Health officials urge the public to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes by taking basic precautions, such as avoiding being outdoors at dawn and dusk, using mosquito repellants and/or wearing long-sleaves and pants to cover the skin. Residents also are encouraged to report dead birds to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s website: myfwc.com/research/wildlife/health/avian. Brevard health officials issue Sept. 3 rabies alert On Thursday (Sept. 3) state health officials issued a rabies alert in Brevard in response to a confirmed case of the viral infection in a raccoon that was captured in the Melbourne area off Andrews Avenue on Aug. 27. "People and domestic animals should always avoid physical contact with wild animals," Florida health officials warned in a press release. That includes raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes, which carry a higher risk of human exposure and a need for rabies post-exposure treatment. "If you are exposed to rabies, receiving appropriate treatment after exposure will protect you from the risk of rabies." The rabies alert is for 60 days and includes the following boundaries in Brevard County: Northern boundary: West Eau Gallie Boulevard Southern boundary: Sarno Road Eastern boundary: Croton Road Western boundary: North Wickham Road Immunize your pets and livestock based on your veterinarian’s recommended schedule. Take the following precautions to prevent rabies exposure: According to Florida Department of Health: Keep pets under direct supervision and on a leash, and keep livestock secured on your property. If an animal bites your pet or livestock, seek veterinary assistance for the animal immediately and contact Brevard County Sherrif’s Office Animal Services at 321-633-2024. Avoid contact with wild or stray animals. Do not handle, feed, or unintentionally attract them with outdoor pet food, open garbage cans, or other sources of food. If you have been bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal, seek medical attention, and report the injury to DOH-Brevard by calling 321-634-6337 option 3. Never adopt wild animals or bring them into your home; instead, contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. Prevent wildlife, including bats, from entering living quarters or occupied spaces in homes, schools, and other similar areas where they might come in contact with people and pets. For information on rabies, please visit FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies or contact DOH-Brevard at 321-634-6337 option 3. Contact Waymer at jwaymer@floridatoday.com. Featured Weekly Ad

supplementary_news.content: Local Sports High School Huddle Scene Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Possible rabies exposure in 7 NC counties after baby goats test positive Iris Seaton Asheville Citizen Times Sept. 1, 2026, 2:19 p.m. ET Rabies was confirmed in three baby goats from a North Carolina mobile petting zoo. The goats were potentially exposed to rabies by a skunk in late July. Anyone who had contact with the goats between July 28 and Aug. 27 may have been exposed. The infected animals were taken to events in at least seven North Carolina counties. Rabies was detected in three baby goats which were in contact with many North Carolina residents through a mobile petting zoo, the N.C. Department of Health and Human Services warned. According to a Friday, Aug. 28 release, the N.C. DHHS and N.C. Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services were first notified of a potential rabies exposure among four baby goats at Farm Adventures in Harmony on Aug. 27. The goats are believed to have been exposed to rabies by a skunk that entered a pen where they were kept in late July. The N.C. State Laboratory of Public Health confirmed rabies in three of the baby goats on Aug. 28. The fourth goat was not tested but is also assumed to have been infected. Officials are working with the farm and impacted local health departments to gather information about potential exposure dates and locations; based on information gathered Aug. 28, it has been determined that no other animals on the farm pose a rabies risk. The infected animals were taken to at least seven NC counties according to latest information from NC agencies. Here's what else to know. Where was rabies detected in North Carolina? Baby goat exposure locations Farm Adventures operates a petting zoo in Harmony, as well as off-site mobile petting zoo events. Anyone who had contact with the baby goats at any location between July 28 and Aug. 27 may have been exposed while the animals were infectious. Impacted individuals should contact their local health department to determine whether medications are needed to prevent infection, and are encouraged to call before visiting an emergency department or urgent care clinic to determine if treatment is needed and where it can be accessed. Known exposure locations where the infected baby goats were taken include: Jurney's Assisted Living, 1942 Van Haven Drive, Statesville, Iredell County - July 28 Private event, Mecklenburg County - July 30 Community Connections Back-to-School Bash, Breeden Amphitheater, 333 S. Main St., Lexington, Davidson County - Aug. 1 Brookdale Peachtree, 2806 Peachtree Road, Statesville, Iredell County - Aug. 6 Private event, Watauga County - Aug. 8 Private event in Burke County - Aug. 9 Masonic Picnic Grounds, 201 Poplar St., Mocksville, Davie County - Aug. 15 Private event, Durham County - Aug. 16 Private event, Iredell County - Aug. 22 Private, Durham County - Aug. 23 Public health officials are working with event organizers to notify attendees who may have had contact with the goats. The investigation is ongoing, with additional information about potential exposure locations to be released when available. Have there been any human rabies cases in North Carolina? The N.C. DHHS statement noted that human rabies infections are "extremely rare" in the U.S., and no human cases have been reported in the state since 2011. How is rabies spread? The N.C. DHHS states that rabies can be spread from wild animals to pets and people primarily through bites, scratches, or infected saliva touching broken skin or mucous membranes. In the case of the infected baby goats, it is possible that people could have been exposed to the virus through saliva from an infected animal. As baby goats are often bottle-fed, handled closely or cuddled, public health officials are "working proactively" to ensure anyone who had direct contact with the affected animals is evaluated. What animals can carry rabies? Though any mammal can carry and spread rabies, Mayo Clinic states that pets and farm most likely to transmit the rabies virus include cats, cows, dogs, ferrets, goats and horses. Wild animals most likely to spread the virus include bats, beavers, coyotes, foxes, monkeys, raccoons, skunks and woodchucks. What are the symptoms of rabies in animals? Humans? Rabies is almost always fatal in mammals, including humans, unless the proper medications are given before symptoms develop. Symptoms can begin weeks to months after someone is exposed. Once the virus enters the body, it travels along the nerves to the brain. Animals with rabies may show a variety of signs. The American Veterinary Medical Association lists the following symptoms as common: Fearfulness Aggression Excessive drooling Difficulty swallowing Staggering Paralysis Seizures Depression, self-mutilation or increased sensitivity to light in horses and livestock Aggressive behavior or unusually affectionate, friendly or fearless behavior Generally unusual behavior, such as nocturnal animals becoming active during the daytime In humans, early symptoms can be flu-like, including weakness, fever or headache as well as a prickling or itching sensation where someone was bitten or exposed. A full list of rabies symptoms among humans from Mayo Clinic includes: Fever Headache Nausea Vomiting Agitation Anxiety Confusion Hyperactivity Difficulty swallowing Excessive salivation Fear brought on by attempts to drink fluids because of difficulty swallowing water Fear brought on by air blown on the face Hallucinations Insomnia Partial paralysis Iris Seaton is the trending news reporter for the Asheville Citizen Times, part of the USA TODAY Network. Reach her at iseaton@citizentimes.com. Featured Weekly Ad
